text:
Well, um... I think there are really two reasons. There's the defensive reason and the inspirational reason.

The defensive one is pretty straightforward. Earth has been around for about 4.5 billion years, and the fossil record is basically a long list of extinction events. Asteroids, supervolcanoes, things we haven't even thought of yet. And we've added a few of our own, like nuclear war and, you know, AI going wrong. So if you look at it from a probability standpoint, any single-planet civilization is going to have *something* bad happen eventually. It's not a question of if, it's when. So we need to become a multi-planetary species. It's like life insurance for consciousness.

And consciousness is, uh... it's really rare, as far as we can tell. We look out at the universe and we don't see anyone else. Maybe we're the only candle in a very dark place. If that's true, we have a duty to keep that candle lit. To extend the scope and scale of consciousness, so we can better understand the nature of the universe and figure out what questions to ask.

But honestly, the second reason matters just as much. You need things that make you excited to wake up in the morning. Life can't just be about solving one miserable problem after another. Becoming a spacefaring civilization, being out there among the stars, that's an exciting future. That's the kind of thing that makes people say, "Yeah, I want to be part of that."

Why Mars specifically? It's the only realistic option. Venus is a high-pressure acid bath, super hot. The Moon is great but it's small, no atmosphere, and the days are a month long. Mars has a 24-and-a-half-hour day, it has water ice, a CO₂ atmosphere you can work with, and enough sunlight. It's a fixer-upper of a planet, but it's doable. You could even terraform it eventually.

The window is the key thing. We've had about 60-something years of spaceflight capability out of 4.5 billion years. That's a tiny window, and it might not stay open forever. So we should make life multi-planetary while we can. That's why we're building Starship: a fully reusable rocket is the fundamental breakthrough you need. If you threw away your 747 after every flight, nobody could afford to fly.

The goal is a self-sustaining city on Mars, one that can keep growing even if the supply ships from Earth stop coming. That's the threshold that matters.

I'd like to die on Mars. Just, uh... not on impact. 😄
